title: Types of Number and Index Laws
kicker: Cambridge Lower Secondary · Mathematics 0862 · Stage 8 · Number
summary: Classify numbers as natural numbers, integers or rational numbers, and use positive and zero indices with the index laws for multiplication and division.

blocks.title: In the curriculum
items: Understand how the natural numbers, the integers and the rational numbers fit inside each other (the hierarchy of numbers) (8Ni.04)
Use positive and zero indices, and the index laws for multiplying and dividing powers of the same number (8Ni.05)

blocks.text: Mathematicians sort numbers into families. Each family sits inside a bigger one, like a box inside a box. In the first part of this page you will learn the three families you need at Stage 8 and how to decide which ones a number belongs to. In the second part you will learn to multiply and divide **powers** quickly using two **index laws**, and why any number to the power 0 equals 1.
Key words

items: natural numbers
الأعداد الطبيعية — the counting numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, …
integers
الأعداد الصحيحة — whole numbers: positive, negative and zero … −2, −1, 0, 1, 2 …
rational numbers
الأعداد النسبية — numbers that can be written as a fraction a/b of two integers (b ≠ 0)
hierarchy
تسلسل / ترتيب هرمي — an order of groups, each one inside the next
terminating decimal
عدد عشري منتهٍ — stops, e.g. 0.75
recurring decimal
عدد عشري دوري — repeats for ever, e.g. 0.333…
base

index form

blocks.text: 1. Natural numbers, integers and rational numbers

items: **Natural numbers** are the counting numbers: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, … (In this course natural numbers start at 1. Some books also count 0 as a natural number; either way, 0 is certainly an integer and a rational number.)
**Integers** are all the whole numbers: the natural numbers, zero and the negative whole numbers: …, −3, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3, …

**Rational numbers** are all numbers that can be written as a fraction a/b, where a and b are integers and b is not 0. This includes every integer (7 = 7/1), every fraction, every **terminating** decimal (0.75 = 3/4) and every **recurring** decimal (0.333… = 1/3).

blocks.text: So the families form a **hierarchy**: natural numbers ⊂ integers ⊂ rational numbers. To decide where a number belongs, ask three questions in order: Is it a counting number? Is it a whole number (positive, negative or zero)? Can it be written as a fraction of two integers?

rows: cannot be written as a fraction

blocks.text: **Look past the appearance.** √16 looks strange but equals 4, a natural number. 20/4 looks like a fraction but equals 5, a natural number. −18/6 = −3 is an integer. Always simplify first, then classify.
Why do we need bigger families?
Each family was needed because some calculations had no answer in the smaller family:

rows: No — can be zero or negative, so we need **integers**
No — can be a fraction, so we need **rational numbers**

blocks.text: **Always, sometimes or never true?** (This is classifying and convincing.) "An integer is a natural number" — **sometimes** (true for 5, false for −5). "A natural number is a rational number" — **always**. "A negative number is a natural number" — **never**. "A rational number is an integer" — **sometimes** (true for 6/3, false for 1/2). To show "sometimes", give one example where it is true and one where it is false.

blocks.text: 2. Powers and index form
A **power** is a short way to write repeated multiplication. In 2^{5} the **base** is 2 and the **index** is 5: 2^{5} = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 32. Also, any number to the power 1 is itself: 9^{1} = 9.
**Careful:** 2^{5} is not 2 × 5. And 2^{10} = 1024 while 10^{2} = 100, so swapping the base and the index changes the value.
3. Index law for multiplication
When you multiply powers of the **same base**, count how many times the base is multiplied altogether:

blocks.title: Division law
blocks.text: a^{m} ÷ a^{n} = a^{m − n}  — same base: **subtract** the indices. Examples: 5^{6} ÷ 5^{2} = 5^{4}; 9^{8} ÷ 9^{3} = 9^{5}; y^{9} ÷ y^{4} = y^{5}. At Stage 8 the first index is always at least as big as the second, so the answer never has a negative index.
5. The zero index

What is 3^{4} ÷ 3^{4}? Any number divided by itself is 1. But the division law gives 3^{4 − 4} = 3^{0}. So **3^{0} = 1**. The pattern below shows the same thing: each time the index goes down by 1, you divide by 2.

blocks.title: Zero index
blocks.text: a^{0} = 1 for any number a that is not 0. Examples: 7^{0} = 1, 100^{0} = 1, (−4)^{0} = 1. It is **not** 0.
6. Using the laws together

items: **A fraction line:** 7^{3} × 7^{5} on top and 7^{6} on the bottom → top = 7^{8}, so 7^{8} ÷ 7^{6} = 7^{2} = **49**.

**Numbers in front (coefficients):** multiply or divide the numbers, then use the index law for the letters. 2a^{3} × 5a^{2} = (2 × 5) × a^{3 + 2} = **10a^{5}**. 12b^{7} ÷ 4b^{3} = (12 ÷ 4) × b^{7 − 3} = **3b^{4}**.
**Missing index:** 4^{☐} × 4^{3} = 4^{9}. The indices must add to 9, so ☐ = **6**.
**Different bases do not combine:** 2^{3} × 5^{2} cannot be written as one power. Work it out: 8 × 25 = **200**.

blocks.text: Worked examples
**Worked example 1** — Complete the table with ticks to show which sets each number belongs to: −5, 3/8, 12, 0.6. [2 marks]

items: −5: a whole number but negative → **integer** and **rational** (−5 = −5/1), not natural.
3/8: not whole → **rational** only.
12: a counting number → **natural**, **integer** and **rational**.
0.6 = 3/5 → **rational** only.
Mark scheme style: 2 marks for all correct; 1 mark for three numbers correct.

blocks.text: **Common mistake:** forgetting that every integer is also rational, so leaving the rational box empty for −5 and 12.
**Worked example 2** — Write down (a) a number that is an integer but not a natural number (b) a rational number that is not an integer. [2 marks]

items: (a) Any negative whole number or 0: for example **−4**.
(b) Any fraction or decimal that is not whole: for example **2/3** or **0.5**.

blocks.text: **Common mistake:** giving 8/4 for (b) — it equals 2, which is an integer.
**Worked example 3** — Simplify, giving each answer in index form: (a) 6^{4} × 6^{5} (b) 9^{8} ÷ 9^{3}. Then (c) work out (2^{5} × 2^{3}) ÷ 2^{6}. [3 marks]

items: (a) Same base, multiply → add indices: 6^{4 + 5} = **6^{9}**.
(b) Same base, divide → subtract indices: 9^{8 − 3} = **9^{5}**.

blocks.text: **Common mistake:** multiplying the indices (6^{20}) or multiplying the bases (36^{9}).
**Worked example 4** — Work out 7^{0} + 4^{0} × 5. [1 mark]

items: Order of operations: 1 + 1 × 5 = 1 + 5 = **6**.

blocks.text: **Common mistake:** thinking a^{0} = 0 and getting 0, or adding first and getting 10.
**Worked example 5** — Find the value of n. (a) 3^{n} × 3^{4} = 3^{10} (b) 5^{8} ÷ 5^{n} = 1 [2 marks]

items: (b) 1 = 5^{0}, so 8 − n = 0 and **n = 8**. (A number divided by itself is 1.)

blocks.text: **Worked example 6** — Hassan says, "2^{3} × 4^{2} = 8^{5}." Explain why Hassan is wrong, and find the correct value. [2 marks]

items: The index laws only work when the **bases are the same**. 2 and 4 are different bases, and the bases are never multiplied together.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
items: Thinking 0 or a negative number is a natural number, or forgetting that integers and natural numbers are also rational.
Classifying by appearance: √16 = 4 and 20/4 = 5 are natural numbers.
Working out 2^{5} as 2 × 5 = 10 instead of 32.
Multiplying the indices when you multiply powers: 3^{4} × 3^{2} = 3^{6}, not 3^{8}.
Multiplying the bases: 3^{4} × 3^{2} = 3^{6}, not 9^{6}. The base stays the same.
Using the index laws with different bases: 2^{3} × 5^{2} is 8 × 25 = 200.
Writing a^{0} = 0. Any non-zero number to the power 0 is 1.

blocks.title: How Checkpoint asks this
items: "Tick the boxes to show which numbers are integers / rational numbers" — a table to complete.
"Write a number that is rational but not an integer" — give a simple example such as 1/2.
"Is this statement always, sometimes or never true?" — give examples as evidence.
"Write as a single power" or "Give your answer in index form" — leave it as, e.g., 5^{7}; do not work it out unless asked.
"Find the value of n" in an index equation — write an equation for the indices, e.g. n + 4 = 10.
"Ring the expressions equal to 1" — look for zero indices and equal powers divided, such as 9^{0} or 4^{3} ÷ 4^{3}.
"Explain the mistake" — name the wrong rule (multiplied the bases / multiplied the indices) and give the correct answer.

blocks.text: Practice

blocks.title: Types of number and index laws practice
blocks.intro: 14 questions, no calculator. For index-form answers, type a power like 4^9. Full solutions appear when you check.

questions.q: Which number is an integer but not a natural number?
questions.e: 7 is natural (and an integer). 2.5 and 1/3 are not whole numbers, so they are not integers. −9 is a whole number but negative, so it is an integer but not a natural number.

c: Every natural number is a rational number.
Every integer is a natural number.
Every rational number is an integer.
Some integers are not rational numbers.
questions.e: Any natural number n can be written as n/1, so it is rational ✓. −2 is an integer but not natural; 1/2 is rational but not an integer; every integer is rational (n = n/1), so the last statement is false.

questions.q: Here is a list of numbers: 6, −2, 0.4, 3/7, 0, 15. How many of them are integers?
questions.e: Integers are whole numbers (positive, negative or zero): 6, −2, 0, 15. That is 4. 0.4 and 3/7 are rational but not integers.
Different bases, so no index law: 2^{3} = 8 and 5^{2} = 25. 8 × 25 = 200.

questions.q: Simplify 4^{6} × 4^{3}. Give your answer in index form (type it like 4^5).
questions.e: Same base, multiplying → add the indices: 4^{6 + 3} = 4^{9}.

questions.q: Simplify 10^{9} ÷ 10^{4}. Give your answer in index form (type it like 10^3).
questions.e: Same base, dividing → subtract the indices: 10^{9 − 4} = 10^{5} (= 100 000).
Any non-zero number to the power 0 equals 1. (8^{3} ÷ 8^{3} = 8^{0}, and any number divided by itself is 1.)
Add the indices: n + 2 = 9, so n = 7.

questions.q: Which of these is equal to 1?
Simplify x^{5} × x^{4}. (Type your answer like x^2.)
questions.e: Same base x, multiplying → add the indices: x^{5 + 4} = x^{9}.

questions.q: Lina says, "5^{3} × 5^{4} = 25^{7}." Explain Lina's mistake and write the correct answer in index form.
questions.ms: 1 mark: explains that the base should stay as 5 / she multiplied the bases (5 × 5 = 25) / you only add the indices. 1 mark: 5^{7} (accept 78 125).
questions.e: When you multiply powers of the same base, the base stays the same and you add the indices. Lina wrongly multiplied the bases. Correct: 5^{3} × 5^{4} = 5^{7}.

questions.q: Ziad says, "If you subtract one natural number from another natural number, the answer is always a natural number." Is Ziad correct? Give an example to support your answer.
questions.ms: 1 mark: No / not correct. 1 mark: a correct counter-example where the answer is zero or negative, e.g. 3 − 8 = −5 (−5 is an integer, not a natural number). The example must be correct for the mark.
questions.e: Ziad is not correct. Example: 3 − 8 = −5, and −5 is not a natural number (it is an integer). It is only sometimes true — e.g. 8 − 3 = 5 is natural. This is why we need the integers.

blocks.title: Remember
items: Natural numbers ⊂ integers ⊂ rational numbers. Every natural number is an integer; every integer is rational (n = n/1).
A rational number can be written as a fraction of two integers: terminating and recurring decimals are rational.
Same base, multiply → add the indices: a^{m} × a^{n} = a^{m + n}.
Same base, divide → subtract the indices: a^{m} ÷ a^{n} = a^{m − n}.
a^{0} = 1 (a ≠ 0). Different bases do not combine — work out each power.
